title: e-Profits: a business-aligned evaluation metric for profit-sensitive customer churn prediction
venue: International Journal of Data Science and Analytics (Springer; ISSN 2364-415X print, 2364-4168 online)
harvard_reference: Manzoor, A., Qureshi, M.A., Kidney, E. and Longo, L. (2026) 'e-Profits: a business-aligned evaluation metric for profit-sensitive customer churn prediction', International Journal of Data Science and Analytics, 22(1), 75. doi:10.1007/s41060-026-01044-6.
abstract_summary: The paper argues that AUC and F1 do not reflect the financial outcome of a retention campaign and proposes e-Profits, a per-customer profit metric: for each customer flagged as a churner the model earns CLV_i minus offer and contact costs if the customer is a true churner, loses the offer and contact costs if a false positive, and earns nothing otherwise. CLV_i = R_i x M / (1 - min(r_i, 0.995)) uses the customer's monthly revenue R_i, a margin M (0.3 in experiments) and a retention probability r_i estimated by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, either tenure-conditioned per customer (TRR: S(T_i + 1)/S(T_i)) or averaged over the population (ARR). Offer cost is 0.1 x CLV_i and contact cost is max(c0, c1 x offer cost). Unlike Expected Maximum Profit (EMP), which assumes fixed population-level CLV, costs and a Beta-distributed acceptance rate, e-Profits gives total and segment-level (e.g. top-20% most valuable customers) profit. Six classifiers (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Explainable Boosting Machine) are benchmarked on the IBM Telco (7,043 rows, 19 features, 26.5% churn) and Maven Telecom (7,043 rows, 32 features, 27% churn) datasets, with hyperparameters tuned by 5-fold cross-validation under five objectives (AUC, Accuracy, F1, EMP, e-Profits) and a fixed 0.5 decision threshold. e-Profits re-ranks the models relative to AUC/F1, reveals financial advantages in models that AUC/F1 overlook, and supports segment-level insight into which model maximises return on high-value customers; code is released on GitHub.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Only partly borne out and the key comparison is absent. Tables 3-4 (arXiv v2 full text) report AUC of 83.5-86.2% on IBM Telco and 91.9-94.3% on Maven for the six tree-based models, with the Explainable Boosting Machine highest (86.16% and 94.16% when tuned on AUC) and RF/XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost within roughly 1-2 points. However, the paper benchmarks ONLY tree ensembles and EBM; logistic regression (or any linear/neural baseline) is not run or discussed anywhere, so it cannot support the statement that tree ensembles are 'top' relative to other model families or 'close to logistic regression'. Cite it for the AUC levels of tree ensembles on these datasets only, and take the LR comparison from another source.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The paper contains no SHAP, permutation-importance or other feature-attribution analysis and reports no ranking of churn drivers; contract type is never analysed. EBM is included because it offers 'a compelling balance between model accuracy and interpretability' (classifier-selection section), but its explanations are not examined. Tenure and monthly revenue appear only as inputs to the metric (tenure conditions the Kaplan-Meier retention probability; monthly revenue feeds CLV), not as identified predictors of churn.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Strongly supported for MODEL choice (not threshold). Abstract: e-Profits 'reshapes model rankings compared to traditional metrics, revealing financial advantages in models previously overlooked by AUC or F1-score'. Results (arXiv v2 Tables 3-4): with AUC-tuned models, EBM has the best AUC/F1 on both datasets, yet Random Forest yields the highest full-population e-Profits (IBM: 9,104,621 vs EBM 7,894,896 under TRR; Maven: 996,582 vs 880,083) and the authors state 'Random Forest achieves higher e-Profits on both the full-population and the top 20% segment, indicating that AUC-optimised models do not necessarily prioritise customers with the highest financial value'. When hyperparameters are tuned on e-Profits instead, XGBoost becomes best (IBM 10,991,460; Maven 1,063,393). Spearman rank correlation between AUC and e-Profits rankings on Maven is only about 0.49 (full population) and 0.45 (top-20%); paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests reject concordance (p<1e-23 Maven, p<1e-18 IBM) and models selected by e-Profits significantly outperform AUC/Accuracy-tuned ones in e-Profits (p<<0.001). Conclusion: 'traditional predictive metrics are insufficient proxies for business value in churn prediction'. Caveat: the paper uses a fixed 0.5 threshold throughout and does not study threshold selection, so it evidences model re-ranking and re-tuning, not threshold change.

claims_supported.claim: Any other specific finding this paper makes that would be useful for a critical discussion of churn prediction methods, imbalance handling, calibration, uplift, survival, fairness or deployment (state it precisely).
claims_supported.where: (1) Survival + profit: retention probability is estimated with a non-parametric Kaplan-Meier curve on tenure (churn = event, non-churners right-censored, non-informative censoring assumed); the tenure-conditioned one-month probability S(T_i+1)/S(T_i) gives customer-level CLV instead of the single population value assumed by EMP (which the paper parameterises as CLV=200, offer cost 10, contact cost 1). (2) Tuning objective matters: models tuned on EMP 'do not consistently maximise e-Profits', and tuning directly on e-Profits lifts the best IBM model from 9,104,621 (AUC-tuned RF) to 10,991,460 (XGB) and the best Maven model from 996,582 to 1,063,393. (3) Segment-level targeting: evaluating on the top-20% most valuable customers changes the winner again (LightGBM 'consistently outperforms other classifiers on top-segment e-Profits when tuned on F1-score, EMP, and e-Profits', e.g. 340,635 on Maven), and in the AUC-tuned IBM block several models record zero top-segment profit, i.e. they flag no profitable high-value customers; the authors argue this makes e-Profits suited to 'resource-constrained retention campaigns'. (4) Explicit limitations (Section 5.2): it is 'a decision-oriented evaluation and model-selection metric rather than a causal treatment-effect estimator'; it assumes every contacted churner is retained and does not model heterogeneous response, so 'integrating causal uplift or treatment-effect modelling' is left to future work; Kaplan-Meier captures heterogeneity 'only through customer tenure using a single population-level survival curve', with Cox proportional hazards (time-varying covariates), Weibull and BG/NBD models suggested as extensions; intervention is binary; results are telecom-only. (5) Methodological choices relevant to critique: fixed 0.5 threshold, no probability calibration, no resampling or class weighting despite 26-27% churn (imbalance addressed only via metric choice), 5-fold CV for hyperparameter selection on the training set followed by refit, profit margin 0.3 and cost-per-offer 0.1 set by assumption. Fairness is not discussed at all.

caveats: Only tree-ensemble and EBM classifiers are compared (no logistic regression, SVM or neural baseline), so the paper cannot be used to rank model families. Decision threshold is fixed at 0.5 and probability calibration is not examined, so profit differences partly reflect how many customers each model flags rather than ranking quality alone. Profit figures depend on assumed parameters (margin 0.3, cost-per-offer 0.1, contact-cost floor) and on the strong assumption that every contacted churner is retained (no uplift/treatment effect). Both benchmark datasets are 7,043-record telecom samples (IBM Telco and Maven Telecom) that appear closely related; check their independence before treating results as two independent benchmarks. The extraction inconsistency on LightGBM's IBM top-20% TRR value means that particular cell should not be quoted without checking the published table.
